claims.text: Retention or loss of toughness is governed by competition between dislocation-mediated plasticity and twinning-induced deformation.
Grain size and phase distribution influence the competition between dislocation-mediated plasticity and twinning-induced deformation.
The initial CoCrFeMnNi-type high-entropy alloy has an FCC crystal structure.
The initial alloy is in an as-cast or wrought condition.
Adding 2 at.% Ti alters the alloy's microstructural characteristics and deformation mechanisms.
The primary test condition is room-temperature, quasi-static tensile loading at a strain rate of 10^-3 s^-1.
Grain size and phase distribution influence dislocation density.
Grain size and phase distribution influence twinning propensity.
The addition of 2 at.% Ti will increase toughness by 15% relative to the baseline.
The predicted toughness increase is caused by grain refinement and an optimized phase distribution.
The baseline alloy without Ti has a Charpy toughness of 120 J/cm^3.
The hypothesis is expected to hold from -20°C to 200°C.
The hypothesis is expected to hold at strain rates from 10^-4 s^-1 to 10^-2 s^-1.
The hypothesis is expected to hold for Ti additions up to 5 at.%.
In-situ neutron diffraction and HRTEM can be used to examine deformation mechanisms and microstructural evolution during tensile testing.
A toughness decrease greater than 10% relative to baseline would falsify the hypothesis.
The absence of significant changes in grain size or phase distribution would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The stated conditions and falsification experiment use quasi-static tensile testing, whereas the predicted toughness outcome is defined by a Charpy impact test. The listed measurements omit Charpy toughness, so the experiment cannot directly evaluate the stated 15% impact-toughness prediction or the toughness-based falsification threshold.
